body.heading: A slide with no way back
paragraphs: Pitcher plants grow in bogs and poor soils across several continents, and they evolved their traps independently in different plant families. The recipe is similar everywhere: a leaf becomes a tube, nectar lures insects to the rim, and a waxy or hairy inner surface makes footing treacherous.

Once an insect slips in, downward-pointing hairs and smooth walls defeat climbing. The pool at the bottom — part rainwater, part plant-made fluid — drowns the prey, and the plant absorbs the nutrients as the body breaks down.

body.heading: Not all pitchers are pitfalls
paragraphs: Some giant tropical pitchers are so large that small mammals visit them. Remarkably, a few of these plants trade instead of trap: tree shrews feed on nectar at the rim and leave droppings that fertilise the plant, while certain bats roost safely inside other pitchers and pay the same rent.
The pitchers show how flexible the plant-animal bargain can be. The same cup shape can be a trap for one visitor and a cafeteria or a bedroom for another.

takeaway: Pitcher plants turn leaves into slippery pitfall cups to harvest nutrients from insects in poor soils.
